sections.html: The charming Eutropius atherinoides grows rarely longer than 6-8 cm. It is quite cheap and available in greater numbers from India. It is a very peaceful inhabitant for every community tank.

The "shark cats" of the genus Pangasius are highly sought after as aquarium fishes because their swimming behaviour resembles a shark. Sadly all species grow very fast and none stays smaller than 50 cm; some reach 150 cm or even more. For some time now so-called "mini-pangasius" have been introduced to the market. One of these species, which from a systematic point of view are not close relatives of Pangasius, is Eutropius atherinoides.
Asia: South central Asia: Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Pakistan. Type locality: Tranquebar.
Inhabits freshwater and tidal rivers, so it tolerates some brackish conditions.
The fish readily takes all types of the usual food for ornamental fishes.
Very peaceful. Plants will not be eaten or destroyed.

Colouration: Silvery greenish along the back with three or four bands along the sides formed by black spots. A black spot on the occiput and another at the base of the dorsal fin.

Description: Pectoral fins long, extending beyond the pelvic fins. Anal fin with 33 to 41 rays.

Taxonomy: Tilak (1964) synonymised this genus under Pseudeutropius and proposed transfer of Pseudeutropius from Schilbidae to Bagridae. Mo (1991) confirmed Tilak's findings and, in the light of his revision of the Bagridae, included Neotropius in it. Two species previously described under Pseudeutropius have also been placed under this genus. The current status is valid as Pachypterus atherinoides, placed in the Horabagridae family. FishBase still lists it in the Schilbeidae, but Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes gives the family Horabagridae.

Etymology: Genus name: Pachys, thick; pterus, fin, allusion not explained, perhaps referring to the considerably more lengthened tail and/or long anal fin (often referred to as Neotropius Kulkarni 1952, a junior synonym). Specific name: –oides, having the form of silversides (Atherinidae: Atherina), probably referring to the silvery stripe on the sides.

IUCN Red List: Although there is no information on the population and its trends, it is still relatively abundant throughout the Indian subcontinent. Despite the lack of understanding of potential threats, it is assessed as Least Concern given its abundance. However, the taxonomy of this species is uncertain and what is now identified as P. atherinoides may consist of more than one species. If so, it will need to be reassessed.
